page: Amazon Web Services r8i.large is a memory-optimized instance powered by the AWS Nitro hypervisor and an Intel Xeon 6975P-C processor. This x86_64 architecture server features 2 vCPUs derived from a single physical core with hyper-threading enabled. It is equipped with 16.0 GB of high-speed DDR5 memory operating at 7 GHz, providing a memory-to-vCPU ratio of 8 GB per vCPU. The processor runs at a clock speed of 3.9 GHz and includes a substantial 480 MB L3 cache, alongside 2 MB L2 and 48 KB L1d caches.

Performance benchmarks reveal strong single-core capabilities, with a Geekbench single-core score of 2163.0 and strong single-threaded compression and decompression throughput, such as 34.33 GB/sec in gzip. However, because the instance is limited to a single physical core, multi-core performance is constrained, as evidenced by a weak Geekbench multi-core score of 2725.0 and a poor stress-ng multi-core CPU result. Memory performance is mixed; while the PassMark memory score is average, large-block uncached read and write bandwidth benchmarks are weak, measuring 20.69 GB/sec and 17.1 GB/sec respectively.

The instance lacks local storage and dedicated GPU hardware, relying entirely on network-attached storage and baseline network bandwidth of 1 Gbps. It supports advanced CPU instruction sets including AVX-512 and Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions for accelerated matrix operations, which aids workloads like lightweight LLM text generation. Qualitatively, the r8i.large offers a cost-effective entry point into the DDR5 memory-optimized class, though it presents a tradeoff between high single-core efficiency and limited multi-threaded scaling. It is best suited for memory-intensive workloads with low parallel processing demands, such as small-scale databases, caching layers, and lightweight enterprise applications.

Powered by a single physical core of an Intel Xeon 6975P-C processor clocked at 3.9 GHz, this x86_64 server utilizes the AWS Nitro hypervisor. It features a large 480 MB L3 cache and supports advanced instruction sets like AVX-512 and Intel AMX. Benchmarks indicate strong single-core performance, highlighted by a Geekbench single-core score of 2163.0 and high single-threaded compression speeds, though multi-core and large-block memory bandwidth benchmarks are relatively weak due to the single-core hardware constraint. Lacking local storage and GPUs, and configured with a 1 Gbps baseline network speed, this instance is qualitatively cost-efficient for memory-bound workloads that do not require heavy parallelization, making it suitable for small databases, caching systems, and basic text-processing applications.
